claim: FSHD is a prevalent myopathy affecting approximately 12 per 100,000 individuals.
source: FSHD is a prevalent (~12/100,000 Deenen et al., 2014), incurable, inherited skeletal myopathy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Deenen et al., 2014

claim: FSHD is characterized by progressive fatty replacement and fibrosis of specific muscle groups driving weakness and wasting.
source: The condition is characterized by progressive fatty replacement and fibrosis of specific muscle groups driving weakness and wasting (Banerji and Zammit, 2021), which is accelerated by inflammation (Dahlqvist et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banerji and Zammit, 2021 and Dahlqvist et al., 2020

claim: FSHD progression is accelerated by inflammation.
source: The condition is characterized by progressive fatty replacement and fibrosis of specific muscle groups driving weakness and wasting (Banerji and Zammit, 2021), which is accelerated by inflammation (Dahlqvist et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dahlqvist et al., 2020

claim: Around 75% of FSHD patients exhibit a descending phenotype with weakness beginning in the facial muscles.
source: Around 75% of patients exhibit a descending phenotype with weakness beginning in the facial muscles, before progressing to the shoulder girdle and latterly lower limb, while the remaining 25% exhibit a range of 'atypical' phenotypes, including facial sparing and lower limb predominant (Banerji et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banerji et al., 2020a

claim: FSHD1 accounts for 95% of cases.
source: Genetically FSHD comprises two distinct subtypes: FSHD1 (OMIM: 158900, 95% of cases) and FSHD2 (OMIM: 158901, 5% of cases).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with OMIM references

claim: FSHD2 accounts for 5% of cases.
source: Genetically FSHD comprises two distinct subtypes: FSHD1 (OMIM: 158900, 95% of cases) and FSHD2 (OMIM: 158901, 5% of cases).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with OMIM references

claim: Both FSHD subtypes share a unifying epigenetic feature: derepression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite at chromosome 4q35.
source: Both subtypes bear a unifying epigenetic feature: derepression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite at chromosome 4q35.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about FSHD genetics

claim: In FSHD1, D4Z4 derepression is due to truncation of the D4Z4 macrosatellite from the typical >100 to 10–1 units.
source: In FSHD1 this is due to truncation of the D4Z4 macrosatellite from the typical >100 to 10–1 units (Lemmers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2010

claim: In FSHD2, derepression is typically due to mutation in SMCHD1.
source: In FSHD2, derepression is due to mutation in a chromatin modifier, typically SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012) but rarely DNMT3B (van den Boogaard et al., 2016) or LRIF1 (Hamanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2012

claim: FSHD2 can rarely be caused by mutations in DNMT3B.
source: In FSHD2, derepression is due to mutation in a chromatin modifier, typically SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012) but rarely DNMT3B (van den Boogaard et al., 2016) or LRIF1 (Hamanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to van den Boogaard et al., 2016

claim: FSHD2 can rarely be caused by mutations in LRIF1.
source: In FSHD2, derepression is due to mutation in a chromatin modifier, typically SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012) but rarely DNMT3B (van den Boogaard et al., 2016) or LRIF1 (Hamanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamanaka et al., 2020

claim: FSHD patients carry permissive 4qA haplotypes distal to the last D4Z4 repeat encoding a polyadenylation signal.
source: In addition to D4Z4 epigenetic derepression, FSHD patients also carry certain permissive 4qA haplotypes distal to the last D4Z4 repeat encoding a polyadenylation signal (Lemmers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2010

claim: Each 3.3 kb D4Z4 repeat encodes the transcription factor DUX4.
source: Each 3.3 kb D4Z4 repeat encodes the transcription factor DUX4, which plays a role in zygotic genome activation, after which it is silenced in somatic tissues (De Iaco et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to De Iaco et al., 2017

claim: DUX4 plays a role in zygotic genome activation and is silenced in somatic tissues.
source: Each 3.3 kb D4Z4 repeat encodes the transcription factor DUX4, which plays a role in zygotic genome activation, after which it is silenced in somatic tissues (De Iaco et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Iaco et al., 2017

claim: Mis-expression of DUX4 protein is believed to underlie FSHD pathogenesis.
source: Mis-expression of DUX4 protein is thus believed to underlie FSHD pathogenesis and DUX4 inhibition is currently the dominant approach to FSHD therapy (Tawil, 2020; Le Gall et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tawil, 2020 and Le Gall et al., 2020

claim: DUX4 inhibition is currently the dominant approach to FSHD therapy.
source: Mis-expression of DUX4 protein is thus believed to underlie FSHD pathogenesis and DUX4 inhibition is currently the dominant approach to FSHD therapy (Tawil, 2020; Le Gall et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tawil, 2020 and Le Gall et al., 2020

claim: DUX4 is extremely difficult to detect in FSHD patient muscle.
source: However, DUX4 is extremely difficult to detect in FSHD patient muscle, with the vast majority of transcript and protein level studies failing to detect DUX4 in FSHD muscle biospies (Banerji and Zammit, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Banerji and Zammit, 2021

claim: When DUX4 is detected in FSHD patient muscle, it requires highly sensitive techniques such as nested RT-qPCR for transcripts.
source: When DUX4 is detected in FSHD patient muscle, it is at very low levels, requiring highly sensitive techniques such as nested RT-qPCR for transcripts (Jones et al., 2012) and proximity ligation assays for protein (Beermann et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al., 2012

claim: Detection of DUX4 protein in FSHD patient muscle requires proximity ligation assays.
source: When DUX4 is detected in FSHD patient muscle, it is at very low levels, requiring highly sensitive techniques such as nested RT-qPCR for transcripts (Jones et al., 2012) and proximity ligation assays for protein (Beermann et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beermann et al., 2022

claim: Single-cell and single nuclear transcriptomic studies find only 0.5–3.8% of in vitro differentiated FSHD myonuclei express DUX4 transcript.
source: Single-cell and single nuclear transcriptomic studies find only 0.5–3.8% of in vitro differentiated FSHD myonuclei express DUX4 transcript (Jiang et al., 2020; van den Heuvel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2020 and van den Heuvel et al., 2019

claim: Immunolabelling studies detect DUX4 protein in between 0.1–5% of FSHD myonuclei.
source: Immunolabelling studies only detect DUX4 protein in between 0.1–5% of FSHD myonuclei (Snider et al., 2010; Rickard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Snider et al., 2010 and Rickard et al., 2015

claim: DUX4 target gene expression is a poor biomarker of FSHD muscle, except in the context of significant inflammation.
source: However, multiple meta-analyses have found DUX4 target gene expression to be a poor biomarker of FSHD muscle, except in the context of significant inflammation (Banerji et al., 2017; Banerji and Zammit, 2019), where it may be confounded by immune cell gene expression (Banerji et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banerji et al., 2017 and Banerji and Zammit, 2019

claim: A recent phase 2b clinical trial of the DUX4 inhibitor losmapimod failed to reach its primary endpoint of reduced DUX4 target gene expression in patient muscle.
source: Importantly, a recent phase 2b clinical trial of the DUX4 inhibitor losmapimod failed to reach its primary endpoint of reduced DUX4 target gene expression in patient muscle, despite improvement in functional outcomes (Jagannathan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jagannathan et al., 2022

claim: The losmapimod clinical trial showed improvement in functional outcomes despite not reducing DUX4 target gene expression.
source: Importantly, a recent phase 2b clinical trial of the DUX4 inhibitor losmapimod failed to reach its primary endpoint of reduced DUX4 target gene expression in patient muscle, despite improvement in functional outcomes (Jagannathan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jagannathan et al., 2022

claim: DUX4 expression in FSHD patient myoblasts follows a burst-like pattern.
source: DUX4 expression in FSHD patient myoblasts follows a burst-like pattern, and cells expressing DUX4 have significantly shortened lifespans, suggesting a gradual attrition of cells over time (Rickard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rickard et al., 2015

claim: Cells expressing DUX4 have significantly shortened lifespans.
source: DUX4 expression in FSHD patient myoblasts follows a burst-like pattern, and cells expressing DUX4 have significantly shortened lifespans, suggesting a gradual attrition of cells over time (Rickard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rickard et al., 2015

claim: A mouse model in which DUX4 expression is induced in a rare burst-like manner bears striking histological and transcriptomic similarities to FSHD patient muscle.
source: A mouse model in which DUX4 expression is induced in a rare burst-like manner bears striking histological and transcriptomic similarities to FSHD patient muscle (Bosnakovski et al., 2017; Bosnakovski et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bosnakovski et al., 2017 and Bosnakovski et al., 2020

claim: DUX4 expression in FSHD patient-derived multi-nucleated myotubes displays a gradient across myonuclei.
source: DUX4 expression in FSHD patient-derived, multi-nucleated myotubes also displays a gradient across myonuclei, suggesting that DUX4 may 'diffuse' either actively or passively from an origin nucleus to neighboring nuclei, bypassing their need to wait for the rare DUX4 burst (Rickard et al., 2015; Tassin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rickard et al., 2015 and Tassin et al., 2013

claim: The half-life of DUX4 mRNA is approximately 2.8 hr.
source: This estimate suggests that the half-life of DUX4 mRNA is approximately 2.8 hr, not atypical for a transcription factor, and on the faster end of the mRNA degradation distribution (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: Calculated from the degradation rate and compared to literature values from Yang et al., 2003

claim: DUX4 mRNA expression was detected in 27/5133 (0.53%) single FSHD myocytes but not in control myocytes.
source: DUX4 mRNA expression was detected in 27/5133 (0.53%) single FSHD myocytes but not in control myocytes (van den Heuvel et al., 2019; Banerji and Zammit, 2019).
evidence: Reported from analysis of scRNAseq data from van den Heuvel et al., 2019

claim: DUX4 positive cells never rose to more than 0.8% of the live cell population in the compartment model simulation.
source: DUX4 positive cells never rose to more than 0.8% of the live cell population and DUX4 target positive cells never more than 2.9%.
evidence: Result from simulating the compartment model over 100 days

claim: DUX4 target positive cells never rose to more than 2.9% of the live cell population in the compartment model simulation.
source: DUX4 positive cells never rose to more than 0.8% of the live cell population and DUX4 target positive cells never more than 2.9%.
evidence: Result from simulating the compartment model over 100 days

claim: There are significant differences in the distributions of cell states between unfused FSHD scRNAseq and syncytial FSHD snRNAseq datasets.
source: Comparing the proportions of myonuclei (cells) assigned to the four live states of our compartment model in the unfused FSHD scRNAseq and syncytial FSHD snRNAseq datasets, we found significant differences in the distributions (Chi-Squared p<2.2 × 10–16, Figure 5A).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 5A

claim: The unfused FSHD myocytes demonstrated a higher proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene -ve susceptible (S) cells compared to syncytial FSHD myonuclei.
source: The unfused FSHD myocytes demonstrated a higher proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene -ve susceptible (S) cells, while the syncytial FSHD myonuclei demonstrated a greater proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene +ve resigned (R) cells.
evidence: Comparison of scRNAseq and snRNAseq data distributions

claim: The syncytial FSHD myonuclei demonstrated a greater proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene +ve resigned (R) cells compared to unfused FSHD myocytes.
source: The unfused FSHD myocytes demonstrated a higher proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene -ve susceptible (S) cells, while the syncytial FSHD myonuclei demonstrated a greater proportion of DUX4 -ve, DUX4 target gene +ve resigned (R) cells.
evidence: Comparison of scRNAseq and snRNAseq data distributions

claim: Differences in proportions of cell states in fused versus unfused myocytes can be explained by the addition of a diffusion term for DUX4 protein.
source: Thus differences in proportions of cell states in fused versus unfused myocytes can be explained by the addition of a diffusion term for DUX4 protein, within the limits of the assumptions of our model.
evidence: Inference from model fitting results

claim: The syncytial compartment model predicts 97% of myonuclei dead by day 10.
source: Simulating the syncytial compartment model over 100 days, we found a much faster death rate than the unfused myocyte model, with 97% of myonuclei dead by day 10.
evidence: Result from simulating the syncytial compartment model

claim: In the syncytial compartment model, DUX4 target gene mRNA expressing cells can comprise up to 70% of living nuclei at 73 hr.
source: DUX4 mRNA-expressing cells remain low in proportion, never exceeding 0.8% of total live nuclei, however, DUX4 target gene mRNA expressing cells can now comprise a significant proportion of living nuclei, up to 70% at 73 hr, though on average comprise only 5.6% of living nuclei (Figure 5F).
evidence: Result from simulating the syncytial compartment model shown in Figure 5F

claim: The cellular automaton model simulation produces an average cell state distribution statistically indistinguishable from the snRNAseq syncytial FSHD myonuclei data.
source: Simulating the cellular automaton model 100 times with this parameter range over 48 hr resulted on average in a statistically indistinguishable approximation of the snRNAseq syncytial FSHD myonuclei state distribution (Chi-squared p=0.98, Figure 6E).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 6E

claim: After restricting DUX4 protein spreading to only neighboring nuclei, the model can still explain the difference between unfused and fused cell state distributions purely with a diffusion term for DUX4 protein.
source: Thus after restricting DUX4 protein from spreading to only neighboring nuclei, we were still able to explain the difference between unfused and fused cell state distributions purely with a diffusion term for DUX4 protein.
evidence: Inference from cellular automaton model fitting results

claim: DUX4 target gene activation is necessary for DUX4-induced cell death.
source: We have previously demonstrated, via a library of DUX4 expression constructs, that DUX4 target gene activation is also necessary for DUX4-induced cell death (Knopp et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knopp et al., 2016

claim: FSHD single myocytes can express DUX4 and DUX4 target genes.
source: FSHD single myocytes can express DUX4 and, therefore, DUX4 target genes (Rickard et al., 2015; Kowaljow et al., 2007; Heher et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rickard et al., 2015, Kowaljow et al., 2007, and Heher et al., 2022

claim: The compartment model assumes that DUX4 target gene expression is stable once activated.
source: There are important assumptions in our compartment model:
evidence: Listed as an explicit assumption of the model

claim: The compartment model assumes that DUX4 protein is stable once translated.
source: There are important assumptions in our compartment model:
evidence: Listed as an explicit assumption of the model

claim: The compartment model assumes that DUX4 target gene positive cells cannot revert to a DUX4 target gene negative state.
source: There are important assumptions in our compartment model:
evidence: Listed as an explicit assumption of the model and evident from model structure

claim: DUX4 is a pioneer factor that increases target gene promoter activation via C-terminal recruitment of p300 to drive H3K27 acetylation.
source: It has been shown that DUX4 is a pioneer factor and increases target gene promoter activation via C-terminal recruitment of p300 to drive H3K27 acetylation (Choi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2016

claim: The model predicts that extremely low levels of DUX4 and target gene expression can drive significant cell death in FSHD myocytes.
source: Our compartment model with experimentally derived parameters thus provides an excellent fit to real-world data and gives a mechanism for how extremely low levels of DUX4 and target gene expression can drive significant cell death in FSHD myocytes.
evidence: Inference from model simulation results

claim: The model suggests that DUX4 target gene expression does not typically increase over time.
source: Moreover, our model predicts that DUX4 target gene expression does not typically increase over time, supporting the finding that DUX4 target gene expression in FSHD muscle has not been validated as a marker of disease progression (Banerji, 2020; Wong et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from model predictions supported by citations to Banerji, 2020 and Wong et al., 2020

claim: Low levels of DUX4 target gene expression may make it difficult to detect changes following anti-DUX4 therapies.
source: Lastly, due to the typically low levels observed, it may be difficult to detect changes in DUX4 target gene activation following anti-DUX4 therapies. This may have contributed to the recent phase 2b trial of losmapimod in FSHD failing to reach its primary outcome measure of suppressing DUX4 target gene expression in patient muscle biopsies (Jagannathan et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculation based on model predictions and clinical trial results from Jagannathan et al., 2022

claim: The model provides an in silico platform to rapidly and cheaply pre-screen anti-DUX4 therapy for FSHD.
source: We thus present our model of DUX4 expression as a theoretical setting to understand the complex dynamics of this important disease gene and as an open source, in silico platform to rapidly and cheaply pre-screen anti-DUX4 therapy for FSHD.
evidence: Stated as the intended application of the model
